definition: Customer relationship management (CRM) is the strategy and software used to organize prospect and customer information, interactions, sales activity, and service history.
extendedDefinition: A CRM gives teams a shared record of people and organizations, including contact details, deal stages, communication history, tasks, and support context. Sales teams use it to qualify leads and forecast pipeline; marketing teams use consent-aware customer segments; service teams use the history to resolve issues without asking customers to repeat themselves. The software only helps when records are accurate, access is appropriate, and teams agree on what each stage and field means. When evaluating a CRM, test data import quality, duplicate handling, permissions, email/calendar sync, reporting, and the cost of required integrations or add-ons. Adoption, migration effort, and ongoing data maintenance matter as much as the feature checklist.
examples: A five-person sales team uses a CRM pipeline to record each opportunity's value, next action, expected close date, and owner, making weekly forecasting more consistent.
A support agent opens a customer record and sees previous tickets and renewal status, so the customer does not need to repeat the same issue.
A marketing team segments customers by consent status and lifecycle stage before sending a campaign, while keeping unsubscribed contacts out of promotional sends.
description: CRM software organizes prospect and customer records, sales pipelines, interactions, and service history. Learn how to evaluate data quality, integrations, adoption, and total cost before choosing a CRM.
